Agent {"subagent_type":"Plan","description":"Design Python intro course plan","prompt":"I need to design a comprehensive reference course for the Tutors platform that teaches Python fundamentals through interactive Jupyter notebooks, Marp slides, and Mermaid diagrams.

## Context

The Tutors platform is a SvelteKit learning management system. Courses are defined as a single `tutors.json` file containing a recursive tree of learning objects. The course will be placed at `D:\code\tutors\test-course-python\tutors.json`.

### JSON Format
Every learning object has: route, type, title, summary, contentMd, frontMatter, id, img, imgFile, video, videoids, hide, authLevel.

- Course (root): adds `properties` and `los` (child topics)
- Topic: adds `los` (child units)
- Unit: adds `los` (child content items)
- Talk (Marp slides): adds `pdf`, `pdfFile`. For Marp: frontMatter must have `{"marp": "true"}` and contentMd starts with `---\nmarp: true\n...`
- Note: markdown content
- Notebook: adds `cells` array and `kernelLanguage` (default "python")
  - Each cell: `{cellType: "markdown"|"code"|"raw", source: string, outputs: [], executionCount: null, metadata: {}, id: string}`
- Lab: adds `los` (LabStep array) and `pdf`, `pdfFile`
  - Each LabStep: `{title, shortTitle, contentMd, contentHtml: "", route, id, type: "step"}`

### Route patterns
- Course: `/course/{{COURSEURL}}`
- Topic: `/topic/{{COURSEURL}}/topic-id`
- Unit: `/topic/{{COURSEURL}}/topic-id/`
- Note: `/note/{{COURSEURL}}/topic-id/unit-id/note-id`
- Talk: `/talk/{{COURSEURL}}/topic-id/unit-id/talk-id`
- Notebook: `/notebook/{{COURSEURL}}/topic-id/unit-id/notebook-id`
- Lab: `/lab/{{COURSEURL}}/topic-id/unit-id/lab-id`

### Key constraint: Interactive notebooks
The user wants notebooks where students can TYPE CODE and solutions. Since the Tutors platform displays notebook cells read-only (rendered from the JSON), the way to make this "interactive" is to include:
- Code cells with example code that students can see and learn from
- Markdown cells with exercise prompts asking students to try things
- Code cells with partial/skeleton code and comments like `# YOUR CODE HERE` for students to fill in mentally or copy to their own environment
- Code cells showing expected output/solutions

## Requirements
Design a course with approximately 8-10 topics covering Python fundamentals, each topic having a mix of:
1. A **Marp slide deck** (talk) introducing the topic concepts
2. A **Jupyter notebook** with hands-on examples and exercises (with `# YOUR CODE HERE` patterns)
3. Where appropriate, a **note** with Mermaid diagrams explaining concepts visually
4. Where appropriate, a **lab** with step-by-step guided exercises

## Topics to cover (in order)
1. Getting Started with Python (setup, first program, REPL)
2. Variables and Data Types (int, float, str, bool, type conversion)
3. Operators and Expressions (arithmetic, comparison, logical, string operations)
4. Control Flow (if/elif/else, match/case)
5. Loops (for, while, range, break/continue, comprehensions)
6. Functions (def, parameters, return, scope, lambda)
7. Data Structures (lists, tuples, dicts, sets)
8. File I/O and Error Handling (open, read, write, try/except)
9. Modules and Packages (import, stdlib, pip, virtual environments)
10. Object-Oriented Programming (classes, inheritance, methods, properties)

## Plan output
Design the complete course structure specifying:
- The full topic/unit/content hierarchy
- For each content item: type, id, title, brief description of what it covers
- For notebooks: outline the cells (markdown explanations + code cells with examples + exercise cells)
- For Marp slides: outline the slides (what each slide covers)
- For notes with mermaid: what diagrams to include
- For labs: what steps to include

Keep notebooks practical and progressive within each topic. The course should feel cohesive — slides introduce concepts, notebooks let students explore, notes visualize relationships, and labs test understanding.","run_in_background":false}

Write {"file_path":"C:\Users\leigh\.claude\plans\buzzing-herding-gray.md","content":"# Plan: Python Fundamentals Reference Course

## Context

Jupyter notebook support was recently added to the Tutors platform. This course will serve as a **reference course** demonstrating notebooks alongside Marp slides, Mermaid diagrams, and labs — showing the full breadth of content types in a cohesive educational experience. The course teaches Python fundamentals to beginners through interactive, practical content.

## Deliverable

A single file: `test-course-python/tutors.json` — a self-contained course following the exact JSON format established by `test-course/tutors.json`.

## Course Structure

**10 topics**, each containing 1 unit with a mix of content types:

| # | Topic | Talk | Notebook | Note (Mermaid) | Lab |
|---|-------|:----:|:--------:|:--------------:|:---:|
| 1 | Getting Started with Python | Y | Y | Y (ecosystem mindmap, execution flow) | - |
| 2 | Variables and Data Types | Y | Y | Y (type hierarchy, conversion flow) | Y (4 steps) |
| 3 | Operators and Expressions | Y | Y | Y (precedence diagram) | - |
| 4 | Control Flow | Y | Y | Y (if/elif/else flow, match comparison) | Y (4 steps) |
| 5 | Loops | Y | Y | Y (loop choice guide) | Y (4 steps) |
| 6 | Functions | Y | Y | Y (function anatomy, LEGB scope) | Y (4 steps) |
| 7 | Data Structures | Y | Y | Y (data structure selector) | Y (4 steps) |
| 8 | File I/O and Error Handling | Y | Y | Y (exception hierarchy, try/except flow) | - |
| 9 | Modules and Packages | Y | Y | Y (import sequence, package structure) | - |
| 10 | Object-Oriented Programming | Y | Y | Y (class diagram, OOP pillars) | Y (5 steps) |

**Totals**: ~56 learning objects (10 talks, 10 notebooks, 10 notes, 6 labs)

## Content Design

### Notebooks (interactive pattern)
Each notebook alternates between:
- **Markdown cells**: Concept explanations and section headers
- **Code cells with outputs**: Working examples students can study (outputs pre-populated as `stream` or `execute_result`)
- **Exercise cells**: Skeleton code with `# YOUR CODE HERE` prompts — students copy to their own Python environment to complete

Typical notebook: 14-22 cells, ~60/40 split markdown/code.

### Marp Talks
10-14 slides per topic. Each uses `frontMatter: {"marp": "true"}` and `contentMd` starting with `---\nmarp: true\ntheme: default\npaginate: true\n---`. Slides introduce concepts that notebooks then explore hands-on.

### Mermaid Notes
Each note contains 1-2 Mermaid diagrams (flowcharts, class diagrams, sequence diagrams, mindmaps) inside fenced ` ```mermaid ` blocks, visualizing key relationships.

### Labs
Step-by-step guided exercises with progressive difficulty. Each step is a LabStep with `type: "step"`, `shortTitle` ("01", "02"...), and `contentMd` containing the exercise instructions.

## JSON Structure Pattern

Every learning object follows the base Lo shape from the test course:
```json
{
  "route": "/type/{{COURSEURL}}/path",
  "type": "...",
  "title": "...",
  "summary": "...",
  "contentMd": "...",
  "frontMatter": {},
  "id": "...",
  "img": "", "imgFile": "", "video": "",
  "videoids": { "videoid": "", "videoIds": [] },
  "hide": false, "authLevel": 0
}
```

Additional fields by type:
- **Talk**: `"pdf": "", "pdfFile": ""`
- **Notebook**: `"cells": [...], "kernelLanguage": "python"`
- **Lab**: `"los": [LabStep...], "pdf": "", "pdfFile": ""`
- **LabStep**: `"title", "shortTitle", "contentMd", "contentHtml": "", "route", "id", "type": "step"`

## Implementation Approach

Due to the sheer size of this file (~4000+ lines of JSON), I'll build it in stages:

1. Create the directory and scaffold the course root + all 10 topic/unit shells
2. Build topics 1-3 with all their content items (talks, notebooks, notes, labs)
3. Build topics 4-6
4. Build topics 7-10
5. Validate the JSON is well-formed

Each topic is self-contained within its `los` array, so building incrementally is safe.

## Verification

1. Run `node -e "JSON.parse(require('fs').readFileSync('test-course-python/tutors.json'))"` to validate JSON
2. Start the dev server (`npm run dev`) and navigate to the course
3. Verify: topics display, Marp slides render, notebooks show cells with outputs, Mermaid diagrams render, labs show steps
4. Spot-check several notebooks for correct cell structure and outputs

Write to file: `D:\code\tutors\test-course-python\topics-1-3.js`

The file should `module.exports = [topic1, topic2, topic3]` where each topic is a plain JS object matching the exact JSON structure below.

## CRITICAL: Exact JSON structure for every learning object

Every single learning object (topic, unit, note, talk, notebook, lab) MUST have ALL of these base fields:
```js
{
  route: "...",        // string
  type: "...",         // string  
  title: "...",        // string
  summary: "...",      // string
  contentMd: "...",    // string (markdown content)
  frontMatter: {},     // object
  id: "...",           // string
  img: "",             // always empty string
  imgFile: "",         // always empty string
  video: "",           // always empty string
  videoids: { videoid: "", videoIds: [] },
  hide: false,
  authLevel: 0
}
```

### Additional fields by type:
- **topic**: add `los: [...]` (array of units)
- **unit**: add `los: [...]` (array of content items)
- **talk** (Marp): add `pdf: "", pdfFile: ""`; set `frontMatter: { marp: "true" }`
- **note**: no additional fields
- **notebook**: add `cells: [...], kernelLanguage: "python"`
- **lab**: add `los: [...], pdf: "", pdfFile: ""` where los contains LabStep objects

### Route patterns (use `{{COURSEURL}}` placeholder):
- topic: `/topic/{{COURSEURL}}/topic-NN-slug`
- unit: `/topic/{{COURSEURL}}/topic-NN-slug/`  (trailing slash!)
- talk: `/talk/{{COURSEURL}}/topic-NN-slug/unit-1/talk-id`
- notebook: `/notebook/{{COURSEURL}}/topic-NN-slug/unit-1/notebook-id`
- note: `/note/{{COURSEURL}}/topic-NN-slug/unit-1/note-id`
- lab: `/lab/{{COURSEURL}}/topic-NN-slug/unit-1/lab-id`

### Notebook cell format:
```js
{
  cellType: "markdown" | "code",  // string
  source: "...",                   // the raw source text
  outputs: [],                     // array - empty for markdown cells
  executionCount: null,            // null for markdown, number for code  
  metadata: {},
  id: "cell-NN-MMM"               // unique: topic number + cell sequence
}
```

For code cells with output, use:
```js
outputs: [{ outputType: "stream", text: "the output\n", name: "stdout" }]
// OR for expressions:
outputs: [{ outputType: "execute_result", data: { "text/plain": "42" }, executionCount: 1 }]
```

Exercise cells should follow this 3-cell pattern:
1. Markdown cell: "## Exercise: Title" with instructions
2. Code cell: skeleton with `# YOUR CODE HERE` comments (no outputs, executionCount: null)
3. Code cell: solution with `# SOLUTION` header comment (include outputs showing the solution working)

### LabStep format:
```js
{
  title: "Step Title",
  shortTitle: "01",
  contentMd: "markdown content for this step...",
  contentHtml: "",
  route: "/lab/{{COURSEURL}}/topic-NN-slug/unit-1/lab-id/01",
  id: "step-01",
  type: "step"
}
```

## TOPIC 1: Getting Started with Python
**id**: `topic-01-getting-started`
**title**: "Getting Started with Python"
**summary**: "Install Python, explore the REPL, and write your first program"

Unit: "Introduction" (id: `unit-1`), contains:

### 1a. Talk: "Welcome to Python" (id: `talk-welcome-to-python`)
Marp slides (10 slides, separated by `---` in contentMd):
1. Title: "Welcome to Python" — subtitle: "Your journey into programming begins"
2. "What is Python?" — high-level, interpreted, dynamically typed, created by Guido van Rossum
3. "Why Python?" — readability, versatility, huge ecosystem, beginner-friendly
4. "Python's History" — 1991, Python 2 vs 3, current Python 3.12+
5. "Installing Python" — python.org, verify with `python --version`, platform tips
6. "The Python REPL" — interactive shell, `>>>` prompt, quick experiments
7. "Your First Script" — `hello.py`, `print("Hello, World!")`, running it
8. "Python IDEs & Tools" — VS Code, PyCharm, Jupyter Notebooks, IDLE
9. "Course Roadmap" — overview of all 10 topics we'll cover
10. "Let's Get Started!" — encouragement, what's next

### 1b. Notebook: "Your First Python Program" (id: `notebook-first-program`)
Cells (aim for ~16 cells):
- Markdown: "# Your First Python Program" intro
- Markdown: "## The `print()` Function"
- Code: `print("Hello, World!")` → output: "Hello, World!\n"
- Code: `print("Hello,", "Python!")` and `print("Line 1\nLine 2")` → outputs
- Markdown: "## Comments"
- Code: showing `# single line` and `"""docstring"""` comments
- Markdown: "## Basic Arithmetic"
- Code: `print(2 + 3)`, `print(10 / 3)`, `print(10 // 3)`, `print(2 ** 10)` → outputs
- Markdown: "## The `input()` Function"
- Code: `name = "Alice"  # simulating input` / `print(f"Hello, {name}!")` → output
- Exercise: "Greeting Program" — ask for name and age, print formatted greeting
- Skeleton + Solution
- Exercise: "Simple Calculator" — two numbers, print sum/difference/product/quotient
- Skeleton + Solution

### 1c. Note: "Python Ecosystem Overview" (id: `note-python-ecosystem`)
contentMd with two Mermaid diagrams:
1. A mindmap showing Python's ecosystem (Web Dev: Django/Flask/FastAPI, Data Science: NumPy/Pandas/Matplotlib, ML: scikit-learn/TensorFlow/PyTorch, Automation: Scripting/Testing/DevOps)
2. A flowchart showing how Python executes code: .py file → Interpreter → Bytecode → Python VM → Output

NO lab for topic 1.

---

## TOPIC 2: Variables and Data Types
**id**: `topic-02-variables`
**title**: "Variables and Data Types"
**summary**: "Understand Python's core data types and how to store values in variables"

Unit: "Core Types" (id: `unit-1`), contains:

### 2a. Talk: "Variables and Data Types" (id: `talk-variables-types`)
Marp slides (12 slides):
1. Title: "Variables and Data Types"
2. "What is a Variable?" — naming a storage location, `=` operator
3. "Naming Rules" — valid names, snake_case convention, reserved words
4. "Integers (`int`)" — whole numbers, arbitrary precision
5. "Floating Point (`float`)" — decimal numbers, precision gotchas
6. "Strings (`str`)" — quotes, triple quotes, escape chars, raw strings
7. "Booleans (`bool`)" — True/False, truthy/falsy
8. "None Type" — `None`, checking with `is None`
9. "Type Checking" — `type()`, `isinstance()`
10. "Type Conversion" — `int()`, `float()`, `str()`, `bool()`
11. "f-strings" — `f"Hello {name}"`, expressions inside `{}`
12. "Key Takeaways" — summary table

### 2b. Notebook: "Working with Variables" (id: `notebook-variables`)
Cells (~20 cells):
- Creating variables (int, float, str, bool) with type() checks → outputs
- Integer arbitrary precision demo: `10 ** 100`
- Float precision: `0.1 + 0.2` gotcha
- String methods: `.upper()`, `.lower()`, `.strip()`, `.split()`, slicing
- Type conversion examples
- f-strings with formatting like `:.2f`
- Exercise: "Personal Info Card" — create variables, print formatted card
- Solution with output
- Exercise: "Temperature Converter" — celsius to fahrenheit
- Solution with output

### 2c. Note: "Type System Overview" (id: `note-type-system`)
Two Mermaid diagrams:
1. classDiagram showing Python type hierarchy (object → int, float, str, bool, NoneType, list, tuple, dict, set)
2. flowchart showing type conversion paths (str→int→float→str, int→bool)

### 2d. Lab: "Variables Practice" (id: `lab-variables-practice`)
4 steps:
1. "Setup" (01): Declare variables of each type, print them with type()
2. "Type Exploration" (02): Use isinstance(), try invalid conversions, discover what happens
3. "String Formatting" (03): Build a formatted receipt using f-strings with alignment
4. "Challenge" (04): Build a Mad Libs program with multiple variable types

---

## TOPIC 3: Operators and Expressions
**id**: `topic-03-operators`
**title**: "Operators and Expressions"
**summary**: "Master arithmetic, comparison, logical, and string operations"

Unit: "Operations" (id: `unit-1`), contains:

### 3a. Talk: "Operators in Python" (id: `talk-operators`)
Marp slides (11 slides):
1. Title: "Operators and Expressions"
2. "Arithmetic Operators" — `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `//`, `%`, `**`
3. "Assignment Operators" — `=`, `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, etc.
4. "Comparison Operators" — `==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`
5. "Logical Operators" — `and`, `or`, `not`
6. "Identity and Membership" — `is`, `is not`, `in`, `not in`
7. "Bitwise Operators" — `&`, `|`, `^`, `~`, `<<`, `>>` (brief)
8. "String Operations" — concatenation, repetition, membership
9. "Operator Precedence" — PEMDAS, precedence table
10. "Expressions vs Statements"
11. "Summary" — quick reference

### 3b. Notebook: "Operator Playground" (id: `notebook-operators`)
Cells (~18 cells):
- All arithmetic operators with outputs
- Comparison operators returning booleans, chained comparisons
- Logical operators, short-circuit demo
- Assignment operators, walrus operator `:=`
- String operations: concatenation, repetition, membership, len()
- Operator precedence puzzles
- Exercise: "Expression Evaluator" — predict outputs before running
- Solution
- Exercise: "Time Converter" — seconds to hours/minutes/seconds using // and %
- Solution

### 3c. Note: "Operator Precedence" (id: `note-operator-precedence`)
One Mermaid flowchart showing precedence hierarchy top-to-bottom:
() → ** → +x -x ~x → * / // % → + - → << >> → & → ^ → | → == != < > → not → and → or

NO lab for topic 3.

---

## Important notes:
- Make ALL content educational, accurate, and beginner-friendly
- Code cell outputs must be realistic and correct
- Use execution counts for code cells that have outputs (1, 2, 3... incrementing per notebook)
- Exercise code cells have `executionCount: null` and empty `outputs: []`
- Solution code cells have `executionCount` set and realistic outputs
- Write substantial content in each Marp slide (not just bullet points — include code examples in slides using markdown code blocks)
- Mermaid diagrams should be syntactically correct
- All strings in JS should use template literals or properly escape newlines for JSON output"}

## TOPIC 4: Control Flow
**id**: `topic-04-control-flow`
**title**: "Control Flow"
**summary**: "Make decisions in your programs with conditional statements"

Unit: "Decisions" (id: `unit-1`), contains 4 items:

### 4a. Talk: "Control Flow" (id: `talk-control-flow`, Marp, 12 slides)
Slides: Making Decisions title → if statement → if/else → if/elif/else → Indentation matters → Truthy/falsy values → Nested conditionals → Ternary expressions → match/case (3.10+) → Pattern matching examples → Guard clauses → Summary

### 4b. Notebook: "Conditional Logic" (id: `notebook-conditionals`, ~20 cells)
- Simple if, if/else, if/elif/else chains with examples and outputs
- Truthy/falsy demo: `bool(0)`, `bool("")`, `bool([])`, `bool(None)` etc.
- Ternary expressions
- match/case with HTTP status codes
- Nested vs flat comparison
- Exercise: "Ticket Price Calculator" — age-based pricing with matinee/3D modifiers → Skeleton → Solution
- Exercise: "Simple Calculator with match/case" — num1, operator, num2 → Skeleton → Solution

### 4c. Note: "Decision Trees" (id: `note-decision-trees`, Mermaid)
Two diagrams:
1. flowchart showing if/elif/else execution flow with branches
2. flowchart comparing if/elif/else vs match/case patterns side by side

### 4d. Lab: "Control Flow Challenges" (id: `lab-control-flow`, 4 steps)
1. "Grading System" (01): numeric score → letter grade with pass/fail
2. "Leap Year Checker" (02): implement leap year algorithm  
3. "Rock Paper Scissors" (03): simple game with conditional logic
4. "Command Dispatcher" (04): match/case text command processor

---

## TOPIC 5: Loops
**id**: `topic-05-loops`
**title**: "Loops"
**summary**: "Iterate over data with for and while loops, and build powerful comprehensions"

Unit: "Iteration" (id: `unit-1`), contains 4 items:

### 5a. Talk: "Loops in Python" (id: `talk-loops`, Marp, 12 slides)
Slides: Repeating Actions title → for loops → range() → while loops → break/continue → else on loops → enumerate()/zip() → Nested loops → List comprehensions → Dict/set comprehensions → Comprehensions with conditions → Choosing the right loop

### 5b. Notebook: "Loop Patterns" (id: `notebook-loops`, ~22 cells)
- Basic for loop over list with output
- range() variations (start, stop, step, negative)
- while loop countdown
- break and continue examples
- enumerate() and zip() 
- Nested loops: multiplication table
- List comprehensions: squares, filtering evens
- Dict and set comprehensions
- Exercise: "Pattern Printer" — nested loops for star patterns → Skeleton → Solution
- Exercise: "Comprehension Challenges" — divisible numbers, word→length dict, grid tuples → Skeleton → Solution

### 5c. Note: "Loop Decision Guide" (id: `note-loop-guide`, Mermaid)
One flowchart: "Need to repeat?" → Know how many times? → Iterating collection? → for/range/while decision tree, with comprehension branch

### 5d. Lab: "Loop Exercises" (id: `lab-loops`, 4 steps)
1. "FizzBuzz" (01): classic 1-100
2. "Number Guessing Game" (02): while loop with hints
3. "Prime Number Finder" (03): find primes up to N
4. "Comprehension Challenges" (04): flatten 2D list, transpose matrix, word frequency

---

## TOPIC 6: Functions
**id**: `topic-06-functions`
**title**: "Functions"
**summary**: "Define reusable blocks of code with parameters, return values, and scope"

Unit: "Building Blocks" (id: `unit-1`), contains 4 items:

### 6a. Talk: "Functions" (id: `talk-functions`, Marp, 13 slides)
Slides: Building Blocks title → Why functions? → Defining a function → Parameters and arguments → *args/**kwargs → Return values → Scope and LEGB → global/nonlocal → Lambda functions → Functions as first-class objects → Type hints → Docstrings → Summary

### 6b. Notebook: "Function Workshop" (id: `notebook-functions`, ~22 cells)
- Defining and calling: greet(name) with output
- Parameters: positional, keyword, default values
- *args and **kwargs examples
- Multiple return values with tuple unpacking
- Scope demo: local vs global
- Lambda functions and usage with sorted()
- Higher-order functions: apply_twice()
- Type hints and docstrings
- Exercise: "Math Utilities" — is_even, factorial, fibonacci → Skeleton → Solution
- Exercise: "Apply Operations" — function that takes list of numbers and list of functions → Skeleton → Solution

### 6c. Note: "Function Anatomy" (id: `note-function-anatomy`, Mermaid)
Two diagrams:
1. flowchart showing function definition parts (def → name → params → docstring → body → return)
2. Nested boxes showing LEGB scope (Built-in > Global > Enclosing > Local) with different colors

### 6d. Lab: "Function Challenges" (id: `lab-functions`, 4 steps)
1. "Basic Functions" (01): is_palindrome, count_vowels, title_case
2. "Parameter Patterns" (02): format_table with *rows, **options
3. "Higher-Order Functions" (03): implement my_map, my_filter, my_reduce
4. "Mini Project" (04): password generator function

---

## TOPIC 7: Data Structures
**id**: `topic-07-data-structures`
**title**: "Data Structures"
**summary**: "Work with lists, tuples, dictionaries, and sets to organize your data"

Unit: "Collections" (id: `unit-1`), contains 4 items:

### 7a. Talk: "Python Data Structures" (id: `talk-data-structures`, Marp, 14 slides)
Slides: Data Structures title → Overview (mutable vs immutable) → Lists → List methods → List slicing → Tuples → Dictionaries → Dict methods → Dict comprehensions → Sets → Set operations → Nested structures → Choosing the right structure → Summary table

### 7b. Notebook: "Data Structure Exploration" (id: `notebook-data-structures`, ~24 cells)
- Lists: creation, indexing, negative indexing, slicing
- List methods: append, insert, remove, sort, pop
- Advanced slicing: [::2], [::-1], shallow copy
- Tuples: creation, unpacking, swap, single-element
- Dicts: creation, access, .get(), iteration
- Dict iteration: .keys(), .values(), .items()
- Sets: creation, union, intersection, difference
- Nested structures: list of dicts
- Starred unpacking: first, *rest = [1,2,3,4,5]
- Exercise: "Contact Book" — dict of dicts with add/find/display functions → Skeleton → Solution
- Exercise: "Student Scores" — zip to dict, find highest, above average, sort by score → Skeleton → Solution

### 7c. Note: "Choosing the Right Data Structure" (id: `note-data-structure-choice`, Mermaid)
Two diagrams:
1. flowchart: Need to store data? → key-value? → dict. Unique? → set. Immutable? → tuple. Else → list
2. graph showing mutable (list, dict, set) vs immutable (tuple, frozenset) groupings

### 7d. Lab: "Data Structure Practice" (id: `lab-data-structures`, 4 steps)
1. "List Operations" (01): implement stack and queue using lists
2. "Dictionary Mastery" (02): word frequency counter
3. "Set Applications" (03): find common/unique elements, deduplication
4. "Student Database" (04): combine all structures for a mini database

---

- Make ALL content educational, accurate, beginner-friendly
- Code cell outputs must be realistic and correct
- Use incrementing execution counts (1, 2, 3...) per notebook for cells that have outputs
- Exercise skeleton cells: executionCount: null, outputs: []
- Solution cells: executionCount set, realistic outputs
- Write substantial Marp slide content (include code examples in fenced blocks)
- contentMd for Marp MUST start with: `---\nmarp: true\ntheme: default\npaginate: true\n---\n\n`
- Mermaid diagrams must be syntactically correct
- Template literals for multiline strings are fine in JS"}

## TOPIC 8: File I/O and Error Handling
**id**: `topic-08-files-errors`
**title**: "File I/O and Error Handling"
**summary**: "Read and write files, and handle errors gracefully with exceptions"

Unit: "Files and Errors" (id: `unit-1`), contains 3 items:

### 8a. Talk: "File I/O and Error Handling" (id: `talk-files-errors`, Marp, 13 slides)
contentMd starts with `---\nmarp: true\ntheme: default\npaginate: true\n---\n\n`
Slides: Title → Opening files (open(), modes r/w/a/x/b) → Reading files (.read(), .readline(), .readlines(), iterating) → The with statement (context managers) → Writing files (.write(), .writelines()) → Working with paths (pathlib.Path) → CSV and JSON (csv module, json.load/dump) → What are exceptions? → try/except → try/except/else/finally → Raising exceptions (raise, custom) → Common exceptions (ValueError, TypeError, FileNotFoundError, KeyError, IndexError) → Best practices (EAFP vs LBYL)

### 8b. Notebook: "Working with Files and Errors" (id: `notebook-files-errors`, ~20 cells)
- Writing to a file with `with open("example.txt", "w")` → output showing success
- Reading from a file → output showing content
- Reading line by line
- Working with JSON: import json, dump dict to file, read it back
- Working with CSV: csv.writer, csv.reader, csv.DictReader examples
- Exception handling basics: try/except ZeroDivisionError
- Full pattern: try/except/else/finally with execution flow
- Handling multiple exceptions

## Context

The Python Fundamentals course has been built with Jupyter notebooks containing exercise skeleton cells (`# YOUR CODE HERE`) and solution cells (`# SOLUTION`). Two problems:

1. **Solutions are visible** — they're rendered as regular code cells, spoiling the exercise for students
2. **Students can't type code** — the notebook viewer is entirely read-only (all cells render as `{@html}`)

## Changes

### 1. Hidden Solutions with "Show Solution" toggle

**How it works**: Solution cells are identified by `metadata.tags` containing `"solution"`. They render collapsed by default with a "Show Solution" button. Clicking reveals the code.

**Files to modify**:

**`src/lib/ui/learning-objects/content/Notebook.svelte`** (~lines 40, 132-150, 175-205):
- Add `revealedSolutions` state (mirrors the existing `revealedOutputs` pattern on line 40)
- Add helper: `isSolutionCell(cell)` — checks `cell.metadata?.tags?.includes("solution")`
- In the sidebar nav (line 132), skip solution cells or show them with a lock/solution icon instead of the normal code icon
- In the main cell rendering (line 175), wrap solution code cells in a collapsible block:
  - When collapsed: show a styled "Show Solution" button (use a distinct color like `warning` to differentiate from the green "Run" button)
  - When expanded: show the full code cell (reuse existing code cell rendering) with a "Hide Solution" button
- Solution cells' outputs follow the same reveal pattern (only visible when solution is revealed)

**`test-course-python/topics-*.js`** (all 3 topic files):
- Add `tags: ["solution"]` to the `metadata` field of every solution code cell
- Regenerate `tutors.json` via `build-course.js`

### 2. Editable exercise cells with CodeMirror

**How it works**: Exercise cells (identified by `metadata.tags` containing `"exercise"`) render as editable CodeMirror editors instead of static HTML. Students can type and modify code directly in the browser. The code is ephemeral (not saved anywhere) — it's a scratchpad for learning.

**Files to modify**:

**`src/lib/ui/learning-objects/content/Notebook.svelte`**:
- Add helper: `isExerciseCell(cell)` — checks `cell.metadata?.tags?.includes("exercise")`
- For exercise cells, instead of rendering `{@html cell.sourceHtml}`, render a `<CodeEditor>` component
- The editor is initialized with `cell.source` as content
- Use a lightweight code editor — CodeMirror 6 (`@codemirror/view`, `@codemirror/lang-python`, `@codemirror/theme-one-dark`)
- The editor value is stored in local reactive state only (not persisted)
- Show a subtle "Exercise" badge on the cell to distinguish it visually

**New component `src/lib/ui/learning-objects/content/NotebookCodeEditor.svelte`**:
- Wraps CodeMirror 6 with Python language support
- Props: `initialSource: string`, `theme: "light" | "dark"` (derived from `currentCodeTheme`)
- Uses `onMount` to initialize CodeMirror (it needs a DOM node)
- Dynamically imports CodeMirror to avoid SSR issues (`import()` inside `onMount`)

**`package.json`** — add dependencies:
- `@codemirror/view`
- `@codemirror/state`
- `@codemirror/lang-python`
- `@codemirror/theme-one-dark`
- `codemirror`

**`test-course-python/topics-*.js`**:
- Add `tags: ["exercise"]` to the `metadata` field of every exercise skeleton code cell
- Regenerate `tutors.json`

## Implementation Order

1. Update topic JS files to add metadata tags (`"solution"` and `"exercise"`) → regenerate JSON
2. Implement solution hiding in `Notebook.svelte` (self-contained, no new deps)
3. Install CodeMirror dependencies
4. Create `NotebookCodeEditor.svelte` component
5. Wire exercise cells to use the editor in `Notebook.svelte`
6. Test both features in the browser

## Verification

1. Navigate to `http://localhost:5173/notebook/localhost:5501/topic-01-getting-started/unit-1/notebook-first-program`
2. Verify solution cells are hidden by default, with "Show Solution" button visible
3. Click "Show Solution" — code and output should appear
4. Click "Hide Solution" — code should collapse

6. Type Python code in the editor — confirm it accepts input
7. Check sidebar navigation — solution cells should show differently
8. Test on a topic with a lab (e.g., topic 2) to ensure labs are unaffected
9. Run `npm run check` to verify no type errors

Traditional online courses present code as static text. This course uses Tutors' new interactive notebook features to let students **write and run Python code directly in the browser** — no local setup required.

### Interactive Exercise Cells

Exercise cells render as fully editable code editors (powered by CodeMirror). Students modify the skeleton code and click **Run** to execute it via [Pyodide](https://pyodide.org/) (Python compiled to WebAssembly). The Python runtime loads once and runs entirely client-side.

### Hidden Solutions with Two-Stage Reveal

Solution cells are hidden by default behind a **Show Solution** button. When clicked, the solution code appears — but the output stays hidden until the student clicks **Run**. This encourages students to read and understand the code before seeing the result.

### Marp Slide Presentations

Each topic opens with a Marp slide deck introducing key concepts. Slides are authored in Markdown and rendered directly in the browser — no PowerPoint or PDF files needed.

### Mermaid Diagrams

Visual notes use Mermaid diagrams (flowcharts, class diagrams, sequence diagrams, mind maps) to illustrate Python concepts like type hierarchies, control flow patterns, and OOP relationships.

## Course Content

| # | Topic | Slides | Notebook | Diagrams | Lab |
|---|-------|:------:|:--------:|:--------:|:---:|
| 1 | Getting Started with Python | 10 | 16 cells | 2 | — |
| 2 | Variables and Data Types | 12 | 20 cells | 2 | 4 steps |
| 3 | Operators and Expressions | 11 | 19 cells | 1 | — |
| 4 | Control Flow | 12 | 21 cells | 2 | 4 steps |
| 5 | Loops | 12 | 23 cells | 1 | 4 steps |
| 6 | Functions | 13 | 23 cells | 2 | 4 steps |
| 7 | Data Structures | 14 | 25 cells | 2 | 4 steps |
| 8 | File I/O and Error Handling | 13 | 23 cells | 2 | — |
| 9 | Modules and Packages | 12 | 21 cells | 2 | — |
| 10 | Object-Oriented Programming | 14 | 25 cells | 2 | 5 steps |

**Totals**: 10 topics, 10 slide decks, 216 notebook cells (20 exercises + 20 solutions), 18 Mermaid diagrams, 6 labs with 25 steps

## How It Works

This course is a single `tutors.json` file — the compiled format that the Tutors reader application consumes. It contains the full course tree: topics, units, talks (Marp slides), notebooks (with cells, outputs, and metadata tags), notes (with Mermaid diagrams), and labs (with step-by-step instructions).

### Cell Metadata Convention

Interactive behavior is driven by standard Jupyter cell metadata tags:

```json
{ "metadata": { "tags": ["exercise"] } }
```

- `"exercise"` — renders as an editable CodeMirror editor with Pyodide execution
- `"solution"` — hidden by default with a two-stage reveal (Show Solution → Run)

Any Tutors course can adopt this convention in its notebook cells.

## Running Locally

1. Clone the [Tutors](https://github.com/tutors-sdk/tutors) reader app and install dependencies
2. Serve this course directory with any static file server:
   ```bash
   npx serve . -p 5501 --cors
   ```
3. Open the Tutors reader and navigate to the course:
   ```
   http://localhost:5173/course/localhost:5501
   ```

## Platform Requirements

The interactive notebook features (exercise cells, solution hiding) require the Tutors reader with the `feat/interactive-notebook-cells` branch merged. Standard Tutors features (Marp slides, Mermaid diagrams, labs) work on the current release.

The output should go into `/tmp/tutors-advanced-python/` (which already has a .git repo - delete everything except .git and README.md first).

## Tutors Source Folder Convention

The folder structure must follow these exact conventions:

### Course root:
- `properties.yaml` — course config
- `course.md` — course description (markdown)

### Topic folders: `topic-NN-slug/`
- `topic.md` — first line is `# Title`, blank line, then summary
- One or more unit folders

### Unit folders: `unit-N/` inside topic
- `unit.md` — single line with unit title text

### Content types inside units:

**Talk (Marp slides):** `talk-N-slug/`
- `talk.md` — line 1: title, line 3: summary
- The Marp content goes in a `.marp` file (e.g. `talk.marp`)

**Notebook:** `notebook-slug/`
- `notebook.md` — line 1: title, line 3: summary (with optional icon frontmatter)
- `notebook.ipynb` — standard Jupyter .ipynb format

**Note:** `note-N-slug/`  
- `note.md` — full markdown content (including mermaid diagrams)

**Lab:** `book-slug/`
- `00.Title.md` — cover page
- `01.Step-1.md`, `02.Step-2.md`, etc. — each lab step's markdown

### .ipynb format:
Standard Jupyter notebook JSON:
```json
{
  "nbformat": 4,
  "nbformat_minor": 5,
  "metadata": {
    "kernelspec": { "display_name": "Python 3", "language": "python", "name": "python3" },
    "language_info": { "name": "python", "version": "3.12.0" }
  },
  "cells": [
    {
      "cell_type": "markdown",
      "metadata": {},
      "source": ["line1\n", "line2\n"],
      "id": "cell-id"
    },
    {
      "cell_type": "code", 
      "metadata": { "tags": ["exercise"] },
      "source": ["code line 1\n", "code line 2"],
      "execution_count": null,
      "outputs": [],
      "id": "cell-id"
    }
  ]
}
```

Note: In .ipynb format, `source` is an array of strings (lines), `cell_type` not `cellType`, `execution_count` not `executionCount`, `output_type` not `outputType`. Metadata tags stay as-is.

## Steps

1. Delete everything in `/tmp/tutors-advanced-python/` except `.git/` and `README.md`

2. Read the tutors.json and create the folder structure. The JSON has this hierarchy:
   - Course root → `los` array of 10 topics
   - Each topic → `los` array with 1 unit
   - Each unit → `los` array with content items (talk, notebook, note, lab)

3. Create `properties.yaml`:
```yaml
credits: Python Fundamentals — A Tutors Reference Course
auth: 0
labStepsAutoNumber: true
```

4. Create `course.md` from the course's `contentMd` field

5. For each topic (indices 0-9), create `topic-NN-slug/`:
   - `topic.md` with `# {title}\n\n{summary}`
   - `unit-1/unit.md` with the unit title

6. For each content item in each unit:

   **type "talk"**: Create `talk-N-slug/`
   - `talk.md`: `{title}\n\n{summary}`
   - `talk.marp`: the raw `contentMd` (which starts with `---\nmarp: true\n...`)
   
   **type "notebook"**: Create `notebook-slug/`
   - `notebook.md` with frontmatter: `---\nicon:\n  type: devicon:python\n---\n{title}\n\n{summary}`
   - `notebook.ipynb`: Convert the cells array from tutors format to standard .ipynb format:
     - `cellType` → `cell_type`
     - `executionCount` → `execution_count`
     - `source` string → `source` array (split by \n, each line gets \n appended except last)
     - `outputType` → `output_type` in outputs
     - Add notebook-level metadata (kernelspec, language_info)
     - Preserve metadata.tags on cells (for exercise/solution)
   
   **type "note"**: Create `note-N-slug/`
   - `note.md`: the full `contentMd` content
   
   **type "lab"**: Create `book-slug/`
   - `00.{title}.md`: A cover page with `# {title}\n\n{summary}`
   - For each step in `lo.los`: `{shortTitle}.{step-title}.md` with the step's `contentMd`

7. Number the talks and notes sequentially within each unit (talk-1, talk-2; note-1, note-2)

Do this carefully — read the full JSON, process every topic, and create all files. Verify at the end that all 10 topics have their content."}

Traditional online courses present code as static text. This course uses Tutors' new interactive notebook features to let students **write and run Python code directly in the browser** — no local setup required.

Solution cells are hidden by default behind a **Show Solution** button. When clicked, the solution code appears — but the output stays hidden until the student clicks **Run**. This encourages students to read and understand the code before seeing the result.

Each topic opens with a Marp slide deck introducing key concepts. Slides are authored in Markdown and rendered directly in the browser — no PowerPoint or PDF files needed.

# Python Fundamentals — A Tutors Interactive Course

A comprehensive introduction to Python programming built for the [Tutors](https://tutors.dev) open-source learning platform. This course showcases three new Tutors capabilities working together: **interactive Jupyter notebooks** with in-browser Python execution, **Marp slide presentations**, and **Mermaid diagrams**.

## What Makes This Course Different

Traditional online courses present code as static text. This course uses Tutors' new interactive notebook features to let students **write and run Python code directly in the browser** — no local setup required.

### Interactive Exercise Cells

Exercise cells render as fully editable code editors (powered by CodeMirror). Students modify the skeleton code and click **Run** to execute it via [Pyodide](https://pyodide.org/) (Python compiled to WebAssembly). The Python runtime loads once and runs entirely client-side.

### Hidden Solutions with Two-Stage Reveal

Solution cells are hidden by default behind a **Show Solution** button. When clicked, the solution code appears — but the output stays hidden until the student clicks **Run**. This encourages students to read and understand the code before seeing the result.

### Marp Slide Presentations

Each topic opens with a Marp slide deck introducing key concepts. Slides are authored in Markdown and rendered directly in the browser — no PowerPoint or PDF files needed.

### Mermaid Diagrams

Visual notes use Mermaid diagrams (flowcharts, class diagrams, sequence diagrams, mind maps) to illustrate Python concepts like type hierarchies, control flow patterns, and OOP relationships.

## Course Content

| 9 | Modules and Packages | yes | 21 cells | yes | — |
| 10 | Object-Oriented Programming | yes | 25 cells | yes | 5 steps |
